title: Pulmonary Function Tests: Pattern Before Label
bottomLine: Interpret PFTs as a pattern: verify test quality, decide whether airflow obstruction is present, assess bronchodilator response in context, and use lung volumes/DLCO to refine restriction, hyperinflation and gas-transfer questions. Never diagnose asthma, COPD or ILD from one spirometry number alone.
recognize: Obstruction is defined by a reduced expiratory ratio relative to the appropriate lower limit of normal, not a universal age-blind cutpoint in every context.
A low FVC on spirometry can reflect restriction, air trapping, submaximal effort or poor technique; lung volumes are needed to confirm true restriction.
differentiate: Bronchodilator responsiveness supports variable airflow physiology but does not by itself prove asthma, and absence of a single positive response does not exclude asthma.
Low DLCO can occur with emphysema, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary vascular disease or anemia; normal DLCO does not exclude every respiratory diagnosis.
assessment: Review smoking/vaping/occupational exposure, symptoms, variability, medications/inhaler withholding, prior PFTs, hemoglobin context, effort/technique and whether testing occurred during an acute illness.
workup: Confirm acceptable/reproducible manoeuvres and interpret spirometry, lung volumes and DLCO according to the clinical question.
Use imaging, bronchoprovocation or specialty testing only when the history and initial physiology justify them.
management: Treat the patient/diagnosis supported by the full clinical picture; repeat testing when response, progression or diagnostic uncertainty makes it useful.
Refer unexplained restriction, disproportionate DLCO reduction, rapidly declining function or discordant symptoms/testing to respirology.
medicationSafety: Do not escalate inhaled therapy solely because one PFT value is abnormal without confirming the diagnosis, technique and adherence.
Medication withholding before testing follows the lab protocol; do not improvise universal withholding intervals.
redFlags: Unexpected restriction/obstruction requiring urgent diagnostic clarification
counselling: Explain that PFTs describe physiology and must be combined with symptoms, exposure history and other tests.
followUp: Trend comparable high-quality tests and avoid overinterpreting small changes near measurement variability.
examTrap: Calling every low FVC 'restrictive lung disease' without confirming total lung capacity.
oneLinePearl: PFTs tell you how the lungs behave; the diagnosis still requires the clinical story.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Pulmonary Function Testing resources

title: Oxygen Therapy: Treat Hypoxemia, Not Dyspnea Alone
bottomLine: Supplemental oxygen treats clinically significant hypoxemia, not breathlessness by itself. Confirm the indication, choose a target appropriate to the disease context, reassess response and carbon-dioxide risk where relevant, and distinguish acute oxygen from long-term home-oxygen qualification.
recognize: Hypoxemia may accompany pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary edema, PE, pneumothorax or other acute disease; oxygen does not treat the underlying cause.
Some chronic hypercapnia-prone patients require controlled oxygen targets and repeat blood-gas assessment when oxygen needs rise.
differentiate: Dyspnea with normal oxygenation may need bronchodilation, diuresis, analgesia, anxiolysis/palliative measures or treatment of another cause rather than oxygen.
Long-term oxygen therapy is based on stable chronic hypoxemia criteria, not a single saturation measured during an acute exacerbation.
assessment: Assess saturation quality, respiratory effort, mental status, perfusion, underlying diagnosis, baseline oxygen, smoking/fire risk and whether hypercapnic respiratory failure is plausible.
workup: Use arterial/venous blood gas when acid-base or hypercapnia information will change care; confirm chronic home-oxygen need when the patient is clinically stable according to the applicable program.
management: Titrate oxygen to the clinically appropriate target while treating the cause of hypoxemia.
Escalate oxygen delivery/ventilatory support when saturation or work of breathing remains unsafe despite initial therapy.
Reassess and wean unnecessary oxygen rather than leaving it indefinitely after the acute problem resolves.
medicationSafety: Oxygen is a drug: excessive exposure can contribute to harm, and uncontrolled high-concentration oxygen can worsen hypercapnia in susceptible patients.
Smoking/open-flame risk with home oxygen requires explicit safety counselling.
counselling: Explain why oxygen may be temporary and why normal saturation does not mean the underlying disease is resolved.
Teach device, flow, fire safety and when worsening breathlessness requires reassessment.
followUp: Reassess oxygen requirement after acute illness and ensure long-term prescriptions meet current local/provincial qualification criteria.
examTrap: Prescribing long-term oxygen from one low saturation during an acute exacerbation without reassessing after stabilization.
oneLinePearl: Oxygen treats hypoxemia; the diagnosis and physiology determine how much and for how long.

title: Respiratory Infection in Immunocompromise: Broaden the Differential Early
bottomLine: In an immunocompromised patient, respiratory infection may progress rapidly and present atypically. Stabilize first, define the type/depth of immune deficit, broaden the organism and noninfectious differential, obtain targeted microbiology/imaging early, and involve acute-care/infectious-disease/respirology expertise sooner than for routine CAP.
recognize: Fever may be absent, inflammatory signs muted and chest radiography initially unrevealing despite serious lower-respiratory disease.
Risk changes with neutropenia, transplant status, corticosteroid/biologic therapy, HIV immune status and recent antimicrobial exposures.
differentiate: Pneumocystis, invasive fungal disease, viral infection, resistant bacteria and mycobacteria become more plausible in selected immune deficits.
Pulmonary edema, drug pneumonitis, diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, malignancy and immune-mediated lung disease can mimic infection.
assessment: Assess ABCs, oxygenation, hemodynamics, immune condition/therapy, transplant timing, neutrophil status, prophylaxis, prior organisms, exposures and recent antibiotics/hospitalization.
workup: Obtain cultures/molecular testing and CT imaging early when severity or host risk justifies it; bronchoscopy or specialized sampling may be needed through specialty care.
Do not delay time-sensitive empiric treatment in an unstable high-risk patient while waiting for every diagnostic result.
management: Use empiric therapy matched to immune defect, syndrome, severity and local epidemiology, then narrow as data return.
Address source control, prophylaxis failures and immunosuppressive medication decisions with the responsible specialty team.
medicationSafety: Renal/hepatic dysfunction and drug interactions are common with antifungal, antiviral and transplant/oncology regimens; medication reconciliation is essential.
Avoid routine corticosteroid escalation for undifferentiated infiltrates until infection and the specific indication are considered.
redFlags: Post-transplant/oncology patient with acute respiratory decline
counselling: Teach low threshold for reassessment because serious infection may not produce typical fever or sputum symptoms.
followUp: Close the loop on cultures, imaging and prophylaxis/immune-therapy changes with the specialty team.
examTrap: Treating an immunocompromised patient's bilateral infiltrates as routine uncomplicated CAP without considering opportunistic infection or noninfectious mimics.
oneLinePearl: Immunocompromise changes both the organism list and how urgently a subtle respiratory syndrome should be taken.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2026 infection-screening position statement for immunosuppressed respiratory patients

title: Thoracentesis: Sample Safely, Know When the Fluid Changes the Plan
bottomLine: Thoracentesis is a diagnostic or therapeutic procedure for selected pleural effusions. Confirm that sampling will change management, use ultrasound-guided/local procedural standards, send fluid studies matched to the differential, and recognize pneumothorax, bleeding and re-expansion complications promptly.
recognize: New unexplained unilateral or atypical effusions often require diagnostic sampling; large symptomatic effusions may benefit from therapeutic drainage.
A known recurrent effusion with a clear cause may not need repeated diagnostic taps if the result will not change care.
differentiate: Transudative and exudative mechanisms guide the differential but do not replace clinical context.
Parapneumonic/empyema, malignant, hemothorax and chylous effusions have different downstream management.
assessment: Assess respiratory status, imaging, effusion size/accessibility, anticoagulants/bleeding risk, platelet/coagulation context, procedure indication and whether another diagnosis/procedure is more appropriate.
workup: Use ultrasound to identify a safe pocket and send pleural fluid cell count, protein/LDH and cause-directed pH, glucose, Gram/culture, cytology or other studies when indicated.
Routine post-procedure chest imaging is not automatically required after every uncomplicated ultrasound-guided thoracentesis; symptoms/procedure events determine need.
management: Stop and reassess if the patient develops chest pain, severe cough, dyspnea, hypotension or another concerning symptom during drainage.
Suspected complicated parapneumonic effusion/empyema requires antibiotics plus prompt drainage/specialty management rather than repeated outpatient observation.
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation/antiplatelet decisions are procedure- and patient-specific; follow current local procedural guidance rather than a universal hold interval.
Avoid excessive rapid drainage when it increases symptom/hemodynamic risk.
counselling: Explain why fluid is being sampled/drained and which post-procedure symptoms require urgent reassessment.
followUp: Track pathology/culture/cytology results to definitive diagnosis and ensure recurrent effusions have an underlying-cause plan.
examTrap: Repeating a thoracentesis because fluid reaccumulated without asking whether the diagnosis is already established and what definitive management is needed.
oneLinePearl: Tap pleural fluid when the result or symptom relief changes care—not because every effusion must be sampled.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society Chest Procedures Working Group resources

title: Occupational Lung Disease: The Exposure History Is a Diagnostic Test
bottomLine: Occupational lung disease is missed when the work history is vague. Identify jobs, tasks, agents, duration/intensity, PPE/controls and the timing of symptoms relative to work, then match objective lung-function/imaging/allergy testing to the suspected exposure and protect the patient from ongoing harmful exposure while the diagnosis is clarified.
recognize: Work-related asthma often improves away from work; pneumoconioses/ILD may present years after exposure; irritant injury can follow a major acute inhalation event.
Construction/mining/silica/asbestos, welding fumes, isocyanates, flour/animal proteins and other exposures create different disease patterns.
differentiate: Occupational asthma requires a work relationship beyond simply having asthma while employed.
Smoking and occupational exposure can coexist; one should not be used to dismiss the contribution of the other.
assessment: Document every relevant job/task, specific agents/materials, ventilation/PPE, coworkers with symptoms, symptom timing on workdays/vacations and smoking/vaping history.
Ask about compensation/reporting context without allowing administrative questions to replace clinical assessment.
workup: Use spirometry/bronchodilator testing, serial peak flow or specialist bronchial/allergy testing for suspected occupational asthma as appropriate.
Use chest imaging and pulmonary-function testing for suspected pneumoconiosis/ILD and involve occupational/respirology expertise when exposure-disease linkage is complex.
management: Reduce/remove harmful exposure when medically indicated and use evidence-based treatment for the resulting lung disease.
Coordinate workplace accommodation, occupational medicine and compensation/reporting requirements according to jurisdiction.
medicationSafety: Escalating inhaler therapy while leaving the patient in a sensitizing exposure can mask deterioration without controlling the cause.
Systemic steroids are not a substitute for removing a dangerous exposure or establishing the diagnosis.
redFlags: Hemoptysis/constitutional symptoms with carcinogenic exposure history
counselling: Explain that exposure control is treatment and that symptoms may persist after sensitization even once exposure stops.
Document workplace recommendations clearly and nonjudgmentally.
followUp: Track symptoms and objective function after exposure modification and close the loop on occupational/respirology referral.
examTrap: Increasing asthma medication repeatedly without asking whether symptoms consistently worsen at work and improve away from exposure.
oneLinePearl: In occupational lung disease, a precise work history can be as diagnostic as a laboratory test.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society respiratory/occupational health resources
Canadian occupational lung disease practice principles
